missions/latin-american-evangelical/name: Latin American Protestant and Pentecostal growth
missions/latin-american-evangelical/stat: Active and still growing in most countries: Pew (2014) found about 19% of Latin Americans identifying as Protestant, most of them Pentecostal or charismatic, and Brazil’s 2022 census recorded about 27% evangélicos. Growth has slowed in some countries as the religiously unaffiliated also increase, and evangelicals have become a major political force.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/summ: Protestantism entered Catholic Latin America with Bible-sellers, immigrants and nineteenth-century missions, but it became a mass movement only when Latin Americans took it over. The Chilean Methodist revival of 1909 and the Swedish-American founders of Brazil’s Assemblies of God in 1911 began a Pentecostal expansion led overwhelmingly by local, often poor and lay pastors. By the early twenty-first century Latin America had tens of millions of evangelicals, a distinctive evangelical theology of ‘integral mission’, powerful neo-Pentecostal corporations such as the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, and a growing presence in politics — together with fierce controversies over prosperity teaching, religious intolerance and alliances with authoritarian power.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/stor:
For three centuries the Iberian Patronato and Padroado excluded Protestantism from Latin America. After independence, Bible-society agents such as the Scot James ‘Diego’ Thomson, who promoted Lancasterian schools and Scripture reading in Buenos Aires, Chile, Peru, Colombia and Mexico between 1818 and 1830, found liberal politicians willing to welcome Protestant ideas. Immigrant churches followed (German Lutherans in Brazil from 1824, Welsh in Patagonia from 1865), and then missions: the Scottish doctor Robert Kalley in Rio de Janeiro (1855), the American Presbyterian Ashbel Green Simonton (1859), Southern Methodists and Southern Baptists (W. B. Bagby at Salvador, 1882). Growth was slow and largely middle-class; Edinburgh 1910 even excluded Latin America as already Christian, provoking the separate Panama Congress on Christian Work in Latin America in 1916.

The decisive change came from revival. In 1909 the Methodist congregation of the American missionary Willis Hoover in Valparaíso, Chile, experienced tongues, visions and ecstatic worship; expelled by the Methodist Episcopal Church, Hoover and his Chilean followers formed the Iglesia Metodista Pentecostal in 1910, which multiplied through street preaching by ordinary members. In 1910 two Swedish Baptist immigrants from the United States, Daniel Berg and Gunnar Vingren, arrived in Belém at the mouth of the Amazon; expelled from a Baptist church for their Pentecostal teaching, they founded in 1911 what became the Assembleias de Deus, Brazil’s largest Protestant body. The Italian-American Luigi Francescon founded the Congregação Cristã no Brasil among Italians in São Paulo the same year.

These churches quickly passed into Latin American hands. Their pastors were workers, peasants and migrants rather than seminary graduates; they preached on street corners, held healing campaigns, met in storefronts and spoke the language and music of the poor. Brazil’s second wave in the 1950s–60s — the Foursquare Church’s tent crusades, Manoel de Mello’s O Brasil para Cristo (1955) and David Miranda’s Deus é Amor (1962) — used radio and mass healing meetings. A third, neo-Pentecostal wave followed with Edir Macedo’s Igreja Universal do Reino de Deus, founded in a former funeral parlour in Rio de Janeiro in 1977, and R. R. Soares’s Igreja Internacional da Graça (1980), which combined deliverance from evil spirits, intense fundraising, television and later political parties.

In Central America, Pentecostalism spread rapidly amid civil wars and natural disasters. In Guatemala, Protestants rose to roughly two-fifths of the population by 2014; the evangelical general Efraín Ríos Montt, an elder of the Church of the Word (El Verbo), ruled in 1982–83 during the worst massacres of Maya villages and was convicted of genocide in 2013 before the verdict was annulled. Among the Maya, Quechua, Aymara and Mapuche, evangelical and Pentecostal churches offered literacy, temperance and leadership, but also provoked conflict with Catholic and traditional communities: in San Juan Chamula, Chiapas, thousands of indigenous Protestants were expelled from their villages from the 1970s onward.

Latin American evangelicals also developed their own theology. The first Latin American Congress on Evangelism (CLADE, Bogotá 1969) and the Latin American Theological Fraternity (founded 1970) gathered thinkers such as René Padilla, Samuel Escobar and Orlando Costas, whose ‘misión integral’ insisted that evangelism and social justice belong together. Their interventions at Lausanne 1974 shaped the Lausanne Covenant’s affirmation of social responsibility and challenged North American church-growth pragmatism. Meanwhile Catholic liberation theology and the Catholic Charismatic Renewal competed for the same poor neighbourhoods; it was often said that ‘the Catholic Church opted for the poor, but the poor opted for the Pentecostals’.

By the 2010s Brazil had more Pentecostals than any other country, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua were around 40% Protestant, and Latin American churches were sending missionaries to Portugal, Africa, Japan and the United States. The evangelical vote (the Brazilian ‘bancada evangélica’ in Congress, support for presidents such as Jair Bolsonaro) became a decisive political factor, and critics pointed to prosperity teaching, financial scandals and attacks on Afro-Brazilian religions; defenders highlighted the movement’s role in giving dignity, community and leadership to millions of the poor, and particularly to women.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/beli: Conversion and personal faith in Christ, in conscious contrast to what evangelicals saw as nominal, sacramental and saint-centred popular Catholicism.
The authority of the Bible, read and preached by lay members in their own words.
Pentecostal baptism in the Holy Spirit, speaking in tongues, divine healing and deliverance from evil spirits.
Strict personal morality — abstinence from alcohol, tobacco, gambling and adultery — which reorganised family economies, especially for women.
In neo-Pentecostal churches, ‘prosperity’ and ‘spiritual warfare’ teaching that links tithes and offerings to God’s material blessing.
In the Latin American Theological Fraternity, ‘integral mission’: the whole gospel for the whole person, uniting evangelism and social justice.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/stra: Street preaching, open-air services and personal testimony by every member, the hallmark of the Chilean Methodist Pentecostals.
Apprenticeship rather than seminary training: pastors rose from the ranks of lay preachers, allowing rapid multiplication of congregations.
Small storefront churches in urban peripheries and rural villages, often within walking distance of members.
Mass healing campaigns, radio from the 1950s and television networks from the 1980s (such as the IURD’s Rede Record, bought in 1989).
Bible translation, literacy and schools among indigenous peoples, often in partnership with SIL/Wycliffe.
Electoral organisation and party-building to defend religious freedom and promote conservative moral policies.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/grou: The urban poor and rural migrants of Brazil, Chile, Mexico and Central America.
Women, who formed a majority of members and found in Pentecostal discipline a means to reform husbands and households.
Indigenous peoples such as the Maya of Guatemala and Chiapas, the Quechua and Aymara of the Andes and the Mapuche of Chile.
Afro-Brazilians and Afro-Latin communities, among whom Pentecostal growth has been especially strong.
Prisoners, addicts and gang members, through rehabilitation ministries in Brazil and Central America.
Latin American migrants in the United States, Spain and Portugal, now a major part of evangelical churches there.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/chal: Legal discrimination and Catholic hostility in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, including violence against Protestants in Colombia during La Violencia (1948–58).
Expulsion of early Pentecostals from Methodist and Baptist churches, and division into numerous small denominations.
Lack of theological education, making the churches vulnerable to authoritarian leaders and doctrinal novelty.
Poverty, violence, civil war and dictatorship in many countries where the churches grew.
The tension between integral-mission thinkers and prosperity or politically partisan leaders within the same movement.
Recent losses to secularisation among young people in Chile, Uruguay and other countries.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/harm: Prosperity teaching and aggressive fundraising, especially in neo-Pentecostal churches such as the IURD, have extracted money from the poor and led to fraud investigations in several countries.

Attacks on Afro-Brazilian religions — from televised demonisation of Candomblé and Umbanda to vandalism of terreiros — and the 1995 televised kicking of a statue of Our Lady of Aparecida by an IURD bishop fuelled religious intolerance.
Support for authoritarian regimes, most notoriously Ríos Montt’s Guatemala (1982–83), and silence about human-rights abuses by some leaders.
Village conflicts in Chiapas and elsewhere, where both sides used violence, expulsions and property seizures.
Concentration of authority and wealth in founder-bishops and family dynasties, with little accountability.
Some foreign mission agencies working among indigenous peoples were accused of facilitating state or corporate penetration of their lands, leading to the expulsion of SIL from several countries.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/deve: Gave millions of poor Latin Americans literacy, community, leadership roles and a sense of dignity independent of patrons and clergy.
Produced a distinctively Latin American evangelical theology — misión integral — that reshaped the Lausanne movement and global evangelical social ethics.
Created the largest national Pentecostal movements in the world, wholly led and financed by Latin Americans.
Contributed to religious freedom and pluralism in historically Catholic states.
Promoted temperance and family stability, which researchers link to improved household welfare among converts.
Turned Latin America into a missionary-sending region, notably through COMIBAM (1987) and Brazilian agencies.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/outc: Latin America changed from an almost exclusively Catholic continent to one where about one person in five is Protestant, mostly Pentecostal, with deep effects on politics, culture and global Christianity.

missions/latin-american-evangelical/coun: From Kalley’s church (1855) to the Assemblies of God (1911) and the IURD (1977), Brazil became the world’s largest Pentecostal nation; the 2022 census recorded about 27% evangelicals.
The Valparaíso revival of 1909 created an autonomous Pentecostal movement that grew to perhaps a sixth of the population by the late twentieth century.
Presbyterian mission from 1882; rapid Pentecostal growth after the 1976 earthquake made Guatemala around 40% Protestant by 2014.
Liberal reforms admitted Protestant missions in the 1870s; Pentecostal and indigenous Protestant growth has been strongest in Chiapas and the south.
Thomson’s schools and later immigrant churches; the healing campaigns of Tommy Hicks (1954) and the 1980s–90s revival under Carlos Annacondia stimulated Pentecostal growth.
Evangelical work among Quechua and Aymara; Samuel Escobar and evangelical students; the evangelical vote mattered in the 1990 election of Alberto Fujimori.
Presbyterians from 1856; Protestants were persecuted during La Violencia (1948–58) but grew rapidly after the 1991 constitution guaranteed religious freedom.
Moravian work on the Miskito coast from 1849 and later Pentecostal growth brought both countries to around 40% Protestant by 2014.
Evangelical missions, radio (HCJB in Quito, 1931) and indigenous Quechua churches transformed highland communities.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/jour: Diego Thomson’s Bible and school journeys through the new republics

Welcomed by independence leaders such as San Martín and Bolívar’s governments, Thomson set up Lancasterian schools using Bible texts as readers and distributed Spanish Scriptures for the British and Foreign Bible Society.
Berg and Vingren sail to Belém

After a prophecy that they were to go to ‘Pará’, the two Swedes sailed from New York and arrived in Belém on 19 November 1910; in June 1911 they and a small group of Baptists expelled with them formed the Apostolic Faith Mission, renamed Assembleia de Deus in 1918.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/rela: Brazilian and other Latin American churches became major missionary senders, organised through COMIBAM from 1987.
Latin American theologians shaped the Lausanne Covenant’s affirmation of social responsibility and the later language of integral mission.
A minority of Latin American Pentecostal churches (Iglesia Pentecostal de Chile, O Brasil para Cristo) joined the World Council of Churches in the 1960s.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/agre: Shared the Azusa-era emphases on Spirit baptism, healing and lay evangelism, though Latin American churches soon became autonomous.
Valued vernacular Scripture, literacy and indigenous-language ministry among Maya and Andean peoples.
Affirmed evangelism as primary while insisting with the Lausanne Covenant that social and political involvement are part of Christian duty.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/disa: Defined itself against the colonial Catholic monopoly and popular Catholic devotion to saints, provoking reciprocal Catholic hostility until well after Vatican II.
Resented Edinburgh 1910’s exclusion of Latin America as already Christian; most Pentecostals later rejected the WCC as liberal and too close to Rome.
Padilla and Escobar criticised the homogeneous unit principle and managerial church-growth techniques as culturally North American and theologically thin.
Chilean Pentecostals were expelled from the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1910 for ‘unscriptural and irrational’ practices.
missions/latin-american-evangelical/devi: Neo-Pentecostal prosperity teaching, which treats offerings as investments in divine blessing, departs from the early Pentecostals’ ascetic and other-worldly piety and from wider Christian teaching on poverty.
Some churches adopted ritual objects (anointed oil, salt, roses, ‘holy’ water) and ‘unloading’ sessions that critics see as reproducing the magical practices they condemned in popular religion.
Political projects aiming at evangelical dominion or partisan alignment contradict the early movement’s refusal of worldly power and its defence of a secular state.
Founder-bishops ruling as unaccountable owners of their churches departed from the Pentecostal ideal of the priesthood of all believers.
